name: Hosea
author: The book is named after Hosea son of Beeri, a prophet: someone believed to speak messages from God to his people. He is the only prophet with a book in the Bible who seems to have come from, and worked in, the northern kingdom of Israel. Little is known of his daily life beyond his troubled marriage to a woman named Gomer, which the book describes. Most take this as a real marriage, though some, both in church tradition and among scholars, have read it as a vision or symbolic story. Most agree the messages go back to Hosea himself, though many scholars think they were later collected and edited in the southern kingdom of Judah, with a few lines added for readers there.
audience: Hosea first spoke to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, which he often calls 'Ephraim' after its leading tribe, and to its leaders in the capital, Samaria. Many mixed worship of Israel's God with worship of Baal, a Canaanite god believed to bring rain and good harvests, and the kingdom's official shrines held golden calf statues. After the north fell, the collected messages were treasured by readers in Judah to the south.
era: Hosea was active from roughly 750 to 720 BC. He began during the long, prosperous reign of King Jeroboam II, but after Jeroboam's death the northern kingdom fell into chaos, with six kings in about 25 years, four of them murdered. The mighty Assyrian empire, based in what is now Iraq, was expanding westward, and Israel's rulers swung between paying it off and seeking help from Egypt. In 722 BC Assyria captured Samaria and carried many Israelites into exile, ending the northern kingdom.

notes.1:1: The opening names kings of Judah from Uzziah to Hezekiah and Jeroboam II of Israel, placing Hosea's work in the second half of the 700s BC.
notes.5:8: Many scholars link this to the war of about 734–732 BC, when Israel and Syria fought Judah and Assyria stepped in; Gibeah and Ramah were border towns.
notes.9:1: This may have been spoken during an autumn harvest festival, when crowds gathered at threshing floors and shrines to celebrate the grain and grape harvests.

flags.problem: The claim that Hosea is the only prophet with a book in the Bible who came from and worked in the northern kingdom is doubtful as worded. Jonah also came from a northern town (Gath-hepher) and is said to have prophesied for Jeroboam II, so a reader who knows this may be confused. Scholars usually make a narrower claim: Hosea is the only prophet from the north whose own messages to the north make up a book.
flags.suggestion: Narrow the claim, e.g. 'He is the only prophet from the northern kingdom of Israel whose messages to his own people fill a book of the Bible.'
